blocks.content: Most lessons sell SOLID as five rules you should always follow. That is only half the story.
Every one of these principles asks you to pay a cost today in return for flexibility tomorrow. Sometimes that trade is brilliant. Sometimes you are paying for flexibility you will never use.
A senior engineer is not the one who applies SOLID everywhere. It is the one who knows when the price is worth it and when it is not.
In this lesson we look honestly at what each principle costs, the hidden tax they all share, and how to decide when to reach for them.
1. Every principle is a trade
SOLID is not free. The thing it buys you is the ability to change code safely. The thing it charges you is more pieces and more indirection.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512828121-824234379.png
blocks.alt: Flow showing a SOLID principle paying a cost of more classes and indirection now, worth it only if the code changes again

blocks.content: One class becomes four. One method call becomes a hop through an interface. A reader who wants to follow the logic now has more files to open. That is the deal you are signing every time you apply a principle.
Good design is not maximum flexibility. It is the right amount of flexibility for the change you actually expect.
So before applying any rule, ask one question: is this part of the code likely to change? If yes, the cost is an investment. If no, the cost is just waste.
2. The cost of SRP
Splitting responsibilities is healthy, until it is not. Push it too far and one simple idea is scattered across a dozen tiny classes.
["More classes and files to create, name, and navigate","Logic that used to live together now spread across the codebase","A reader has to assemble the full picture from many small pieces"]
items: More classes and files to create, name, and navigate
Logic that used to live together now spread across the codebase
A reader has to assemble the full picture from many small pieces

blocks.content: A class that does four unrelated jobs is a problem. But ten classes that each do almost nothing, just to pass data along, is also a problem. That is called fragmentation, and it can hurt readability as much as a God Class.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512830224-185596224.png
blocks.alt: Spectrum from a God class with too few classes, through a balanced split, to fragmentation with too many tiny classes

blocks.content: The balance
Split by reason to change, not by line count. If two pieces of logic always change together, leaving them in one class is the simpler and better choice.
3. The cost of OCP
Open Closed asks you to add an abstraction so future behaviour can be plugged in without editing old code. The catch is that you usually add it before you know what the future needs.

Here the interface, the extra class, and the wiring all earn their keep only if more discount types arrive. If they never do, you paid for flexibility nobody used. This mistake is so common it has a name: speculative generality.
Guessing the future wrong is more expensive than a small edit later. When in doubt, wait for the second case before you generalise.
4. The cost of LSP
Liskov keeps your inheritance honest, but honest hierarchies are hard to design. Real world things rarely fit a clean parent and child relationship.
Forcing a hierarchy that almost works leads to fragile base classes and surprising subclasses. Often the cost of getting inheritance right is higher than simply avoiding it.
The balance

When a subclass struggles to honour its parent, that is a signal to prefer composition over inheritance. Hold an object and delegate to it instead of extending it. The LSP problem disappears because there is no parent contract to break.
5. The cost of ISP
Splitting fat interfaces into focused ones is good, but every split adds another type to your system.
["More interfaces to name, track, and implement","A single class may now implement several small interfaces at once","Taken too far, you get one interface per method, which is just noise"]
items: More interfaces to name, track, and implement
A single class may now implement several small interfaces at once
Taken too far, you get one interface per method, which is just noise

blocks.content: The goal is interfaces shaped around what callers actually need, not the largest possible number of interfaces. One clean interface with three related methods usually beats three interfaces with one method each.
6. The cost of DIP
Dependency Inversion gives you the most freedom and charges the highest tax: indirection.
When everything depends on interfaces, reading the code no longer tells you what actually runs. You see an interface call, but the real implementation is wired in somewhere else entirely.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512831921-822716734.png
blocks.alt: Caller code going through an interface while the concrete implementation that actually runs is wired in elsewhere

blocks.content: ["Harder to trace a call to the concrete code that runs","More wiring and setup, often pushed into a DI framework","Extra ceremony that can overwhelm a small or simple project"]
items: Harder to trace a call to the concrete code that runs
More wiring and setup, often pushed into a DI framework
Extra ceremony that can overwhelm a small or simple project

blocks.content: Indirection is a loan. It buys flexibility now and charges interest every time someone reads the code.
The balance
Invert the dependencies that are likely to change or that you need to fake in tests, such as databases and external services. Do not wrap stable, internal logic in interfaces just to follow the rule.
7. The hidden tax they all share
blocks.text: 7. The hidden tax they all share

blocks.content: Notice the pattern. Every principle trades simplicity now for flexibility later, and the currency is almost always indirection and more moving parts.

That tax is invisible on the day you write the code and very real on the day someone new tries to read it. A pile of interfaces and tiny classes can be just as hard to understand as one giant method, only in the opposite direction.
Over engineering and under engineering both make code hard to change. The target is the middle, not either extreme.
8. When the trade is worth it
blocks.text: 8. When the trade is worth it

blocks.content: Use this simple test before applying a principle:

["Does this code change often? If yes, flexibility pays off. If no, keep it simple.","Do I have a real second case, or am I guessing? Wait for the second case before you abstract.","Will this make the code easier or harder to read for the next person? Readability usually wins.","Do I need to fake this in a test? If yes, an abstraction earns its place."]
items: Does this code change often? If yes, flexibility pays off. If no, keep it simple.
Do I have a real second case, or am I guessing? Wait for the second case before you abstract.
Will this make the code easier or harder to read for the next person? Readability usually wins.
Do I need to fake this in a test? If yes, an abstraction earns its place.

blocks.content: SOLID pays off most in code that lives a long time and changes a lot: core domain logic, shared libraries, anything many people touch. It pays off least in throwaway scripts, prototypes, and stable corners that nobody edits.
9. Common questions

If SOLID has costs, should I stop using it? No. SOLID is still one of the best tools you have for managing change. The point is to apply it on purpose, where change is likely, instead of everywhere out of habit.

How do I know if I am over engineering? A good sign is when the abstraction has exactly one implementation and has had only one for a long time. If the flexibility is never used, it was probably premature.

Do these principles ever conflict with each other? Yes. Aggressive SRP can push you toward many tiny classes, which can fight readability. Heavy DIP adds indirection that SRP splitting already increased. Balancing them against each other is exactly the skill this lesson is about.

What should I optimise for if not the principles themselves? Optimise for code that is easy to change and easy to read. The principles are means to that end, not the end itself. When a rule stops serving those two goals, set it aside.

SOLID is a set of trades, not commandments. Once you can see the cost on each side, you stop asking "does this follow the rule?" and start asking "is this worth it here?" That question is what separates clean design from cargo cult design.
10. The file and interface explosion

Every principle we covered adds at least one file: an interface, a strategy class, a factory. Multiply that by five principles applied everywhere, and a small feature can spawn a dozen files before a single line of business logic runs.

Take a simple order confirmation email. In a codebase that applies SOLID without judgement, that one action can require an interface, an implementation, a factory, and a service that only exists to hold the wiring, four or five files for a call that could have been three lines in an existing class.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512835250-347218352.png
blocks.alt: One simple action fanning out into an interface, a factory, a wiring service, and an implementation before reaching the real logic

blocks.content: Why individually simple classes get collectively hard
blocks.text: Why individually simple classes get collectively hard

blocks.content: Each of those files is trivial in isolation. Read any one of them and you understand it in seconds. The difficulty is not in any single class, it is in tracing behaviour across all of them. To answer what happens when an order confirms, you now open a factory, follow it to an interface, follow that to an implementation, and check where the wiring is configured.
Local simplicity does not add up to global simplicity. A codebase can be full of small, tidy classes and still be one of the hardest systems to onboard onto.

["A new hire needs a map, not just readable files, to find where behaviour actually lives","Debugging a call chain means jumping through several files instead of scrolling one","Renaming or deleting a class means checking every interface and factory that references it","Code review takes longer because a small feature touches many small files at once"]
items: A new hire needs a map, not just readable files, to find where behaviour actually lives
Debugging a call chain means jumping through several files instead of scrolling one
Renaming or deleting a class means checking every interface and factory that references it
Code review takes longer because a small feature touches many small files at once

blocks.content: None of this makes any single file wrong. It becomes a real cost when the number of files a codebase carries grows faster than the number of behaviours it actually needs to support. A feature that has had exactly one implementation for two years is paying rent on rooms nobody moved into.
11. Selective application: where experienced engineers spend the budget
blocks.text: 11. Selective application: where experienced engineers spend the budget

blocks.content: Experienced engineers do not apply SOLID uniformly across a codebase. They treat indirection as a limited budget and spend it where change is likely, not everywhere the rule technically applies.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512837232-324656826.png
blocks.alt: Decision framework asking whether code changes often or needs a test double before spending the abstraction budget

blocks.content: Where the flexibility earns its keep
blocks.text: Where the flexibility earns its keep

blocks.content: ["Payment and billing logic, because providers and pricing rules change often","Integrations with third party APIs, because vendors get replaced","Anything under active experimentation, such as ranking or ordering logic","Code that must be swapped out in tests, such as clocks, storage, and network calls"]
items: Payment and billing logic, because providers and pricing rules change often
Integrations with third party APIs, because vendors get replaced
Anything under active experimentation, such as ranking or ordering logic
Code that must be swapped out in tests, such as clocks, storage, and network calls

blocks.content: In contrast, a plain class with no interface is usually the better choice for internal utilities that have not changed in years, one-off scripts and migrations, glue code that only calls two other services in sequence, and anything with a single, well-understood implementation that nobody expects to replace.

The skill is not knowing the five letters of SOLID, it is knowing which slice of the codebase will actually need to flex and reserving the abstraction budget for that slice instead of spending it everywhere out of habit.
12. Worked example: technically SOLID, practically overengineered
blocks.text: 12. Worked example: technically SOLID, practically overengineered

blocks.content: Consider a notification feature that only ever needs to send an order confirmation by email. Below is a version that satisfies every SOLID principle on paper.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512838957-443711934.png
blocks.alt: Overengineered notification design compared with the pragmatic single class version, promoted to an interface only if a second channel arrives

blocks.content: This code ticks every box. NotificationSender is a narrow interface, so it respects ISP. EmailNotificationSender is the only implementation, but new channels can be added without touching existing code, which is OCP. NotificationService depends on the abstraction rather than the concrete class, which is DIP. Each class also has exactly one reason to change, which is SRP. It has also never needed a second implementation in the eighteen months since it shipped.
The pragmatic middle ground
The pragmatic version skips the interface and the factory entirely, because there is only one channel and no test double is needed beyond mocking the mail client itself.

If a second channel, SMS or push, actually arrives, promoting the pragmatic version to an interface is a small change: extract the method signature into an interface, rename the class to something like EmailOrderNotifier, and add the new implementation beside it. That is far cheaper than carrying an unused interface and factory for eighteen months on the chance a second channel might show up.

{"pros":["Fewer files to read for a single, well-understood flow","Adding a second implementation later is a small, mechanical refactor","A new engineer can trace the entire flow inside one file"],"cons":["If a second channel does arrive, some churn is needed to introduce the interface","Slightly less resistant to accidental tight coupling if the class grows carelessly over time","Requires the discipline to extract an abstraction promptly once real variation shows up, rather than never"]}

The pragmatic version is not the opposite of SOLID, it is SOLID applied with judgement. The single responsibility is still respected, the class still has one reason to change. What was dropped is the abstraction that had no second implementation to justify it.
